heading: Network Services for Growing Businesses
intro: Start with the problem: slow Wi-Fi, a new office or move, an aging firewall, no backup Internet, or no one watching the network. We scope the fix around your site, team and budget—every engagement is custom-quoted after a free consultation.

seo.title: Seattle Network Services: Wi-Fi, Office Setup, Security & Backup Internet | Reliable IT Consulting
seo.description: Problem-led network services in Greater Seattle: slow Wi-Fi fixes, office setup and moves, firewall/VPN security checkups, backup Internet, cabling, monitoring and Network Care. Custom quotes.

items.a: We serve businesses across the Greater Seattle Area, including Seattle, Bellevue, Redmond, Kirkland, Renton, Issaquah, Bothell, Lynnwood, Everett and Tacoma. Remote consulting is also available.
Every engagement is custom-quoted. After a free consultation we scope the work around your site, equipment and goals, then confirm the quote in writing before work begins.

items.q: Do you work with small offices as well as larger organizations?
items.a: Yes. Typical projects range from 5–50-person office network and Wi-Fi deployments to multi-site and enterprise network engineering, including routing, switching, SD-WAN and cloud networking.
Yes. We provide clear communication and documentation in both English and Mandarin.

items.q: Which network technologies do you work with?
items.a: We regularly work with Cisco, Juniper, Palo Alto, Fortinet, Aruba, Ubiquiti and Meraki equipment, and we are vendor-neutral when recommending new hardware.

items.q: Why is our office Wi-Fi slow even though we pay for fast Internet?
items.a: Internet speed is only one link in the chain. Slow Wi-Fi is often caused by access-point placement, channel interference, roaming problems, overloaded APs, weak switching/PoE, or cabling. We test wired vs wireless first so you do not buy the wrong fix.

items.q: Do we need Wi-Fi 7, or is Wi-Fi 6/6E enough?
items.a: For many offices, Wi-Fi 6/6E is still enough. Wi-Fi 7 helps most in dense, high-capacity environments—and only when client devices, switches, PoE, cabling and uplinks can support it. We recommend based on your devices and bottlenecks, not the newest label.

items.q: What happens to our business if the Internet goes down?
items.a: Without a continuity plan, POS, cloud apps, phones and cameras can all stop together. A backup-Internet design adds a second ISP or 5G/LTE failover, UPS protection for core network gear, priority rules for critical traffic, and a tested outage runbook.

items.q: How do we separate guest Wi-Fi, POS, cameras and office computers?
items.a: They should not share one flat network. We design separate network segments (such as VLANs) with firewall rules so guests can reach the Internet without reaching office computers, POS systems, cameras or printers.

items.q: Our VPN is slow or keeps disconnecting. What are the options?
items.a: The fix depends on the bottleneck: firewall throughput, Internet upload speed, VPN settings, split tunneling, or the remote-access design itself. We review the current VPN first, then recommend repair, replacement, or an identity-based remote-access option if it fits.

items.q: What should be ready before our office move?
items.a: Start the ISP order early, count network drops from the floor plan, confirm rack location/power/UPS, run and test cabling before furniture blocks access, and test Internet, Wi-Fi, VPN, phones and printers before staff move in.

guides.heading: Network Know-How: Problems, Explained Plainly
guides.intro: You do not need to become a network engineer. These are the distinctions we use when diagnosing a business network—and what we check before recommending new equipment.

items.title: Slow Internet is not the same as slow Wi-Fi
items.body: If a wired computer is fast but wireless devices drop or crawl, the Internet line may be fine. The problem could be access-point placement, channel interference, roaming, the switch or PoE budget, or the cabling behind the AP.
items.check: Wired vs wireless speed tests, coverage map, AP/switch health, channel and roaming behavior.

items.title: More access points can make Wi-Fi worse
items.body: Too many APs turned up too loudly can cause devices to cling to a distant AP or roam at the wrong time. Good Wi-Fi is a design—coverage, capacity, channels and transmit power working together—not just more hardware.
items.check: Site survey, channel plan, AP placement, transmit power, and post-install validation with real devices.

items.title: Wi-Fi 7 is a system decision, not a sticker
items.body: New APs only help if the rest of the system keeps up: client devices, switch ports, PoE budget, cabling and Internet uplink. Many offices get more value from fixing design and backhaul than from jumping to the newest standard.
items.check: Device mix, AP generation, 2.5G/PoE switch readiness, cabling condition, and where the real bottleneck is.

items.title: Guest Wi-Fi should never touch POS or office computers
items.body: A single flat network means a guest phone, a camera, a POS terminal and your file shares all live in the same neighborhood. Segmentation keeps the convenience of guest Wi-Fi without giving it a path into business systems.
items.check: VLAN/segmentation design, firewall rules between segments, and who can administer each network.

items.title: A slow VPN is not always an Internet problem
items.body: VPN performance can be limited by the firewall, upload bandwidth, tunneling settings, or forcing all traffic through the office. In other cases the better fix is a different remote-access design with MFA and per-user access.
items.check: Firewall throughput and firmware, VPN configuration, MFA, user/vendor access list, and split-tunnel policy.

items.title: A backup line only counts if it has been tested
items.body: A second Internet connection sitting in a box does not help if failover was never tested, the firewall has no power during an outage, or staff do not know what to do. Continuity means the failover, the UPS and the runbook all work together.
items.check: Failover test, UPS coverage for core gear, priority traffic rules, and a one-page outage runbook.
